summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

primary_citations.citation_text: District of Columbia - D.C. Code Title 4, Chapter 13, Subchapter I, Part A (Reporting Abuse and Neglect) — §§ 4-1301.04, 4-1301.06 investigation and findings

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Probable cause supported the medical hold and shelter care of an infant with suspected shaken baby syndrome and the parents' Child Protection Register listing did not violate due process, but the warrantless seizure of the sibling from inside the family home was remanded for a determination whether exigent circumstances existed.
key_cases.relevance: It states the D.C. rule that emergency removal requires a court order, probable cause or exigency, and applies it to a hospital medical hold.
key_cases.quote: under the Fourth Amendment, a lawful seizure of children from their parents' custody requires a court order, e.g., a warrant, probable cause, or exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The District failed to carry its burden of showing that shelter care was necessary for a healthy five-month-old removed after her mother's hospitalization, even under the less demanding probable cause standard, so the shelter care order was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a parent's untreated mental health issues, without evidence of likely danger to the child, cannot justify emergency removal.
key_cases.quote: Because we conclude that the District failed to carry its burden even under a less-demanding probable-cause standard, we assume without deciding that a probable-cause standard applies.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Only the child, not the parent, may take an interlocutory appeal from a shelter care order under D.C. Code § 16-2328(a), and that limitation does not violate due process because the custody deprivation is temporary and followed by a factfinding hearing at which the government must prove its allegations by a preponderance.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a parent has no immediate appeal from the emergency removal and shelter care decision.
key_cases.quote: Because it is not the child who has brought this appeal (but rather her mother), we lack jurisdiction to entertain it under the plain language of the statute.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The warrantless entry into the apartment and seizure of an infant taken from a hospital nursery were justified by emergency circumstances, so the identification of the baby and the ensuing confession were not suppressed and the kidnapping conviction was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: It is the presumption against warrantless home entry that an emergency removal decision must overcome.
key_cases.quote: Fourth Amendment law presumes that warrantless searches and seizures inside a home are unreasonable absent exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
key_cases.holding: Individual District caseworkers had qualified immunity on the Fourth and Fifth Amendment claims because the contours of the exigency exception for warrantless child removals were not clearly established, but summary judgment for the District itself was vacated and remanded for Monell analysis of the removal policies.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that in an exigency the District may seize children without a court order, but leaves the standard for exigency unsettled in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: the precise contours of when an exigency exists to justify removal without a warrant or pre-deprivation hearing are not settled

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: An unwed father was constitutionally entitled to a hearing on his fitness before his children were taken from him, and Illinois' presumption that unwed fathers are unfit denied him due process and equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: It condemns removal decisions made by presumption rather than by individualized proof about this parent.
key_cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him
